# Social Media Goals: Examples and How to Set Them


November 12, 2026 • 16 MIN READ


Authors


Aishwarya Suresh is an experienced content writer specializing in social media management, social listening, social analytics, Voice of the Customer (VoC) and customer experience. She writes practical, research-backed guides that help brands understand customer conversations, measure social media performance and turn insights into meaningful business decisions.


[View full bio](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/author/aishwarya-suresh/)


**Key Takeaways:**


- Social media management drives results when every post ties back to a business goal, not when it simply keeps the feed active.
- Strong management rests on five connected pillars: content, scheduling, community, listening and analytics, working as a system.
- AI now handles the operational layer, freeing managers to focus on brand judgment and voice.
- Social has become a discovery channel, so content built to be found and understood matters as much as content built to engage, not just to reach.
- Consolidating publishing, listening and analytics on one governed platform helps teams move faster and stay on-brand, not stitch point tools together.


Social media goals are the business outcomes your social program is accountable for: demand, revenue, customer loyalty, reputation and, how your brand shows up when customers ask AI for a recommendation. The strongest goals today aren't channel targets like follower growth. They measure how well social turns customer conversations into results for marketing, customer care and the wider business.


That's harder than it sounds, because most teams only measure what happens on their own channels. Sprinklr's[2026 Social Index Report](https://www.sprinklr.com/resources/social-index-report/) found that in telecom, sentiment on brands' owned channels and sentiment in earned media were 115 percentage points apart. What a brand sees on its own feed can be a very different story from what customers say everywhere else.


That blind spot is getting more expensive. When a buyer asks ChatGPT or Google's AI Overviews which brand to shortlist, the answer often draws on forum threads, reviews and creator content, not your brand page. So what people say about you on social now shapes recommendations you'll never see in your native analytics.


This guide covers eight goals worth setting, each with a SMART example and the KPIs that prove progress. You'll also learn how to set targets that survive a quarterly review and how to track them across channels, brands, and regions.

##


What are social media goals?


Social media goals are specific, measurable outcomes a brand wants its social media activity to deliver, such as awareness, engagement, website traffic, leads, sales, better customer service, a stronger reputation or a larger community. Each goal connects a business objective to a target, a metric, and a deadline.


A useful goal passes three checks:


- It supports something the business already cares about, like pipeline, retention, or launch awareness.
- It has a baseline and a number, so progress is visible.
- It has a date, so the team knows when to review it.


"Grow our Instagram" fails all three. "Lift Instagram engagement rate from 2% to 3% by the end of Q1 to support the spring launch" passes them.


The list of outcomes has widened in 2026. Teams now also set goals for visibility in social search and AI-generated answers, because more people start their research there (more on this in the examples below).


***What is the difference between social media goals, objectives, and KPIs?***


A goal is the broad outcome you want social to contribute to, such as "increase brand awareness." An objective is the specific, measurable target inside that goal, such as "grow share of voice in our category from 18% to 23% by the end of Q3." A KPI (key performance indicator) is the metric that shows whether you're moving toward the objective, such as share of voice, reach or brand mentions.


One more distinction trips teams up: every KPI is a metric, but not every metric is a KPI. Your dashboard may show 40[social media metrics](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-metrics/) . Only the handful tied to an active goal deserve a place in your leadership report.


##


Why social media goals matter


Without clear goals, social media becomes a content treadmill: posts go out, engagement fluctuates, and no one can confidently answer " *what did this achieve?* " Goals create the connective tissue between daily execution and strategic outcomes. They help teams focus resources on the channels and formats that matter, justify budget requests with evidence, plan content around intended outcomes, and report to stakeholders in language they understand — revenue, retention, and reputation.


Here's where goals make the biggest practical difference:


· **Focus:** Goals tell your team which platforms, formats and audiences deserve attention, and which ones can be dropped.


· **Budget decisions:** When spend is tied to a target, it's easier to justify investment and shift money toward what's working.


· **Content planning:** A clear goal decides your content mix. An awareness goal calls for reach-friendly video. A lead goal calls for proof points and offers.


· **Performance tracking:** Goals define which KPIs matter, so you stop reporting everything and start reporting what moved.


· **Stakeholder reporting:** Leadership wants to know what social did for the business. Goals give you a direct answer.

##


Common social media goals with examples


Most brands work toward a mix of the eight goals below. For each one, you'll find what it means, a SMART example you can adapt, and the KPIs worth tracking. The numbers in the examples are placeholders, so swap in your own baselines.


### 1. Increase brand awareness


[Brand awareness](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/brand-awareness/) is about getting more of the right people to see, recognize and remember your brand. For many teams it is the first goal to set, because awareness feeds every later stage of the funnel, and when people are ready to buy, they start with the brands they already know. It is also increasingly shaped by how often a brand shows up in social search and AI-generated answers.


**SMART example:** Increase our share of voice against our top three competitors from 18% to 23% across Instagram, TikTok and LinkedIn by the end of Q3.


**KPIs to track:**


**Reach:** The number of unique people who saw your content. Learn how it differs from impressions in our guide to reach vs. impressions.


- **Impressions:** How many times your content was displayed.
- **Share of voice:** Your brand's share of all conversation in your category.
- **Brand mentions:** Tagged and untagged mentions across social, forums and news.
- **Video views and completion rate:** How much of your short-form video people actually watch.


**How Sprinklr helps:**[Sprinklr’s competitive insights and benchmarking tool](https://www.sprinklr.com/products/consumer-intelligence/competitive-benchmarking/) compares your social performance with competitors, and[Social Listening](https://www.sprinklr.com/products/consumer-intelligence/social-listening/) tracks brand mentions across millions of data sources.


### 2. Increase engagement


Engagement measures how actively people interact with your content through comments, shares, saves and replies. It feeds most other goals, because traffic, community and leads all start with someone choosing to interact. Test formats such as creator content, short-form video and replies in comments to see what earns interaction.


**SMART example:** Raise average Instagram engagement rate from 2% to 3% by the end of Q1 by moving 30% of posts to short-form video and creator content.


**KPIs to track:**


- **Engagement rate:** Total engagements divided by reach or impressions.
- **Comments and replies:** A sign your content sparks real conversation.
- **Shares and saves:** Content people want to pass on or come back to.
- **Average watch time:** How long people stay with your videos.
- **Click-through rate** , when traffic is the intended next step.

### 3. Drive traffic to your website


**What it means:** Sending social audiences to your website, landing pages or product pages. Attribution is the sticking point here, because platforms such as Instagram and TikTok limit where clickable links can go. Pair link-friendly placements such as LinkedIn posts, YouTube descriptions and link-in-bio pages with consistent UTM tagging.


**SMART example:** Grow social-referred sessions to our product pages by 25% (from 12,000 to 15,000 a month) by the end of Q3, tracked through UTM-tagged links in Google Analytics 4 (GA4).


**KPIs to track:**


- **Click-through rate (CTR):** The share of people who clicked your link after seeing the post.
- **Social-referred sessions:** Visits to your site that came from social channels.
- **Engagement rate in GA4:** The share of sessions where visitors actually engaged with your site, which is the inverse of bounce rate.
- **Average engagement time:** How long social visitors stay active on your site.
- **Cost per landing-page** visit for paid campaigns.


**How Sprinklr helps:** If your site analytics run on Adobe, the[Adobe Customer Journey Analytics](https://www.sprinklr.com/help/articles/adobe-customer-journey-analytics-cja/integrate-adobe-customer-journey-analytics-cja-with-sprinklr/6a38c58c9643895377852b32/) integration combines Adobe and Sprinklr data into one cross-channel report.


### 4. Generate quality leads


The goal of[social media lead generation](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-lead-generation/) is to capture potential customers and move them into your sales pipeline. That can happen through native lead forms, gated content, webinar sign-ups, or newsletter subscriptions. The word that matters most here is "quality." A thousand leads that never convert do more harm than good, so tie this goal to what sales actually accepts.


**SMART example:** Generate 400 marketing-qualified leads (MQLs) from LinkedIn lead gen forms and organic posts in the second half of the year, at a cost per lead under $90.


**KPIs to track:**


- **Lead form submissions:** Leads captured through native forms and landing pages.
- **Cost per lead (CPL):** Total spend divided by leads generated.
- **Lead-to-MQL rate:** The share of social leads that meet your qualification criteria.
- **Content downloads and event sign-ups:** Interest signals from gated assets and webinars.


**How Sprinklr helps:**[Sprinklr’s Employee Advocacy platform](https://www.sprinklr.com/products/social-media-management/employee-advocacy-platform/) can amplify brand reach by turning employees into advocates, and in addition you get AI-personalized content recommendations for every advocate. Its[Social Marketing for Distributed Teams](https://www.sprinklr.com/products/social-media-management/distributed-marketing-platform/) feature helps local teams and sellers generate leads while headquarters keeps control of brand and compliance.


Lead goals aren't only about brand accounts anymore. Employees and advisors often have more trust with buyers than a brand page does.


### 5. Increase conversions and revenue


Conversion goals measure social's direct impact on revenue, whether that happens through paid campaigns, shoppable posts, creator partnerships or retargeting. Optimizing[social media campaigns](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-campaigns/) , targeting the right audiences and pairing paid with creator content all help turn interest into purchases.


**SMART example:** Achieve a 4:1 return on ad spend (ROAS) on paid social prospecting campaigns for the fall collection by November 30, while keeping cost per acquisition under $35.


**KPIs to track:**


- **Conversion rate:** The share of social visitors who complete a purchase or desired action.
- **Revenue attributed to social:** Total sales driven by social channels.
- **Return on ad spend (ROAS):** Revenue generated for every dollar spent on ads.
- **Cost per acquisition (CPA):** What it costs to win one customer through social.
- **Average order value (AOV):** The average value of purchases that come from social.

Recent releases added more control over TikTok Smart+ campaigns, the ability to create and manage OpenAI ads, and a pre- and post-boost comparison view (limited availability).[Conversational Commerce](https://www.sprinklr.com/teams/customer-service/conversational-commerce/) turns social chats into a revenue channel.


As creator content takes a bigger share of budgets, it helps to see creator, paid and organic results side by side. ### 6. Improve social customer service


Customers expect to get help where they already are, and for many people that means a DM or a public reply on social. A[social customer service](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-customer-service/) goal focuses on responding quickly, resolving issues in the channel, and turning frustrated moments into loyal customers. Every public reply is also a reputation moment, because other customers are watching.


**SMART example:** Cut median first response time on X and Facebook from four hours to under one hour by the end of Q2, while keeping customer satisfaction (CSAT) at or above 85%.


**KPIs to track** (more in our guide to[social customer service metrics](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-customer-service-metrics/) ):


- **First response time:** How long customers wait for your first reply.
- **Resolution rate:** The share of issues fully resolved on social.
- **SLA compliance:** The share of conversations handled within your target time.
- **Customer satisfaction (CSAT):** Survey-based ratings after an interaction.

[Santander UK](https://www.sprinklr.com/stories/santander-uk/) handles about 3,000 inbound social messages a week on Sprinklr, and the bank broke down silos between its marketing and customer care teams along the way.


### 7. Protect and grow brand reputation


Reputation goals focus on how people feel about your brand, not just how often they mention it. That means tracking sentiment, catching negative spikes early, and responding before a complaint becomes a crisis. Reputation is shaped as much by conversations you don't own (reviews, forums, creator videos) as by your own posts, so listening matters as much as publishing here.


**SMART example:** Keep net sentiment at or above +30 through Q4 and respond to 90% of negative mentions within two hours.


**KPIs to track:**


- **Sentiment:** The balance of positive, negative, and neutral mentions over time, measured through[sentiment analysis](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/sentiment-analysis/) .
- **Share of negative mentions:** An early warning sign worth watching week to week.
- **Time to detect:** How quickly your team spots a spike in negative conversation.
- **Share of voice:** How your reputation compares to competitors in the same conversations.


**How Sprinklr helps:** Sprinklr's AI classifies sentiment in 100+ languages, and Sprinklr's[social listening](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-listening/) surfaces shifts before they escalate.[Stage Entertainment](https://www.sprinklr.com/stories/stage-entertainment/) used it to gauge how audiences felt about returning to theaters after lockdowns, then built its content around what visitors were saying. With[automatic spam account detection](https://www.sprinklr.com/help/articles/sprinklr-ai/detect-spam-and-impersonation-profiles-with-ai-studio/6a5df264ca4012abef53aa03/) , AI flags brand risks and non-compliant content before a post goes live.


***How do AI search and social search change social media goals in 2026?***


They add visibility as a goal. People look for brands on TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Reddit, and AI assistants answer brand questions using what the web and social say about you. An[Adobe Express survey](https://searchenginejournal.com/gen-z-preference-for-tiktok-over-google-drops-50-data-shows/568267) from early 2026 found that 49% of US consumers had used TikTok as a search engine, although Gen Z's preference for TikTok over Google fell from 8% to 4% between 2024 and 2026, so social search sits alongside Google. Trusted sources such as LinkedIn and Reddit also shape the signals AI assistants use to evaluate and recommend brands, which makes consistent publishing and community engagement part of the awareness goal.


In practice, add one or two visibility KPIs to your awareness goal: appearances in social search results, branded search volume and the share of AI answers that mention your brand for your priority prompts. A SMART example is raising the share of AI answers that mention your brand across ten priority prompts from 18% to 30% by June 30.


### 8. Grow an engaged community


Community growth is different from follower growth. A large following that never interacts is an audience. A community is a group of people who come back, talk to each other, create content about your brand, and defend it when it matters. Building a[brand community](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/brand-community/) takes longer, but it compounds into loyalty, user-generated content and word-of-mouth that paid media can't buy.


**SMART example:** Grow your Facebook Group from 8,000 to 12,000 active members by September 30, while keeping the share of members who post or comment each month above 15%.


**KPIs to track:**


- **Follower growth rate:** Net new followers as a percentage of your total audience.
- **Repeat engagers:** People who interact with your content regularly.
- **User-generated content (UGC) volume:** Posts customers create about your brand.
- **Employee advocacy reach:** How far your content travels through employee networks.


**How Sprinklr helps:** Community management and Employee Advocacy features in[Sprinklr Social](https://www.sprinklr.com/products/social-media-management/) help you build and grow communities around the brand.


Remember, these are just a few examples to inspire your ideas. The key is to align your social media goals with your business objectives and choose KPIs that directly measure your progress toward those goals.


##


How to set SMART social media goals


SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. The framework is decades old, but it still works because it forces you to replace "do better on social" with something your team can plan around, and leadership can review. Before you write one, do two things: confirm the business objective social is meant to support, and pull your baseline for the last three to six months. You can't set a credible target without knowing where you start.


**SMART element**


**What it means on social**


**Example**


Specific


Name the outcome, the platform, and the audience. Avoid catch-all goals like "grow on social."


Increase LinkedIn engagement among IT decision-makers in North America


Measurable


Attach a KPI and a number, starting from your current baseline.


Lift engagement rate from 2.5% to 3.5%


Achievable


Check the target against your history, platform benchmarks, and team capacity.


A one-point lift is realistic with two new content series a month


Relevant


Connect the goal to a business priority leadership already cares about.


Supports the pipeline target for the new security product line


Time-bound


Set a deadline and checkpoints so progress can be reviewed.


By the end of Q3, reviewed monthly


A simple sequence helps teams get from objective to goal:


1. Start with the business objective, such as launching a product, lowering support costs, or growing pipeline.


2. Pull your baseline from native analytics and your social dashboard, so targets rest on real numbers.


3. Choose one primary goal and one lead KPI for each objective.


4. Write the goal in SMART form, for example: "Increase average Instagram engagement rate from 2% to 3% by June 30 by shifting 30% of posts to short-form video."


5. Break it into monthly milestones and give it an owner.


[Sprinklr Copilot](https://www.sprinklr.com/products/platform/sprinklr-copilot/) can summarize performance in your dashboards and explain sudden shifts, which helps when you are setting baselines. For the wider plan around your goals, see this guide to building a[social media strategy](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-strategy/) .


***How many social media goals should you set at once?***


Most teams do best with one primary goal and one or two supporting goals per quarter. Every extra goal splits your content, budget and attention, and quarterly reviews quickly turn into a list of half-explained numbers. Pick the goal that matters most to the business right now, then add supporting goals that feed it. For example, an engagement goal can support a lead goal by warming up the audience you later retarget.


Larger organizations can run more goals in total, but each one should have a clear owner. A regional team might own awareness, the care team owns response time, and the demand team owns leads, with all of them rolling up to the same dashboard.


##


How to track progress toward your social media goals


A simple measurement routine keeps goals on track. Three habits cover most of it:


· **Start with native analytics and GA4.** Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, YouTube and X analytics show post-level reach, engagement and audience data. In GA4, tag every social link with UTM parameters so traffic lands in the Organic Social or Paid Social channel groups instead of showing up as direct or referral, and set key events such as form submissions and purchases so you can tie visits to your goals.


· **Bring channels into one tool and one dashboard.** A[social media management tool](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-management-tools/) with reporting and dashboards puts every channel against the same targets, so you can see progress on each goal without exporting from five platforms. Build one view per goal with the baseline, target and deadline on it, and share it with stakeholders. These[social media reports](https://www.sprinklr.com/blog/social-media-reports/) are a good starting point.


· **Review on a fixed cadence.** Check post-level results, response times, and anomalies weekly. Compare goal KPIs against target and decide what to scale or stop every month. Rebaseline and reset goals every quarter.


***What is a realistic social media growth goal?***


A realistic growth goal starts from your own data, not a number that sounds good in a planning meeting. Look at your average performance over the last three to six months, compare it with benchmarks for your industry and platform, and factor in what your team can actually produce. A steady improvement on a strong baseline is more credible, and more achievable, than a dramatic target built on hope.


It also helps to set ranges rather than single numbers. A "commit" target you're confident of hitting and a "stretch" target that requires everything to go right gives leadership a realistic picture and gives your team room to experiment.
